hints: Focus on how atomic size changes down Group 17 and how that affects holding onto electrons and forming strong bonds.
Remember that iodide loses an electron much more easily than chloride, and that chlorine with fewer electrons has weaker London forces than bromine.
Connect the thermal stability of $\text{HX}$ to how easily the $\text{H-X}$ bond breaks on heating, so compare $\text{H-Br}$ with $\text{H-I}$.
walkthrough:
**Recall the key Group 17 trends**

Down the group, atoms get larger and the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded. This makes electron loss easier but electron gain and covalent bond overlap poorer.

Trend summary:
$$\text{reducing power of } X^- \text{ increases: } \text{Cl}^- < \text{Br}^- < \text{I}^-$$
$$\text{bond strength of H-X decreases: HF > HCl > HBr > HI}$$

**Check volatility and reducing power**

Volatility depends on intermolecular forces. $\text{Cl}_2$ is smaller with fewer electrons than $\text{Br}_2$, so it has weaker London forces, lower boiling point and higher volatility. Reducing power depends on ease of oxidation. $\text{I}^-$ is largest so it loses an electron most easily.

$$\text{I}^- \rightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}\text{I}_2 + e^- \text{ (easiest, strongest reducing agent)}$$

**Check thermal stability and reactivity**

Thermal decomposition of hydrogen halides requires breaking the $\text{H-X}$ bond. A shorter, stronger bond needs more heat to break, so $\text{HBr}$ is more stable than $\text{HI}$. Halogen reactivity ($\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$) is about gaining electrons, not about having a weak $\text{X-X}$ bond, a weak bond would actually make breaking easier.

options.A: Incorrect. Reducing strength increases down the group. $\text{I}^-$ is larger and its outer electron is lost most easily, so iodide is a much stronger reducing agent than chloride.
options.B: Incorrect. Chlorine is more volatile (gas at room temperature while bromine is a liquid) because it has weaker, not stronger, intermolecular London forces due to fewer electrons and a smaller electron cloud.
options.C: Correct. Bond length increases and orbital overlap worsens from Br to I, so the $\text{H-Br}$ bond is stronger with a higher bond enthalpy than $\text{H-I}$. More heat is needed to break it, so $\text{HBr}$ resists thermal decomposition better than $\text{HI}$.
options.D: Incorrect. It is true iodine is less reactive than bromine, but the reason given is backwards. A weaker $\text{I-I}$ bond would make bond breaking easier. Lower reactivity down the group is due to lower electronegativity and less tendency to gain an electron, not weak covalent bonds.
